post1.text:
Most companies that stall between $50M and $500M do not have a strategy problem. They have a leadership problem they have mislabeled as a strategy problem.

When companies like Strive Health expand their executive teams specifically to scale a core mission, they are not just filling seats. They are making a structural bet that the right leaders at the right levels determine whether growth actually holds.

Here is what scaling leaders need to internalize:

1. The leadership behaviors that got you to $50M will actively work against you past it. Founders who cannot delegate decisions at speed become the bottleneck.

2. Culture does not scale on its own. It scales because someone with authority over resources protects it under pressure.

3. Hiring executives to scale is not the same as developing leaders who can scale. One is procurement. The other is strategy.

The companies that make it to $500M and beyond treat leadership architecture as seriously as their financial model.

What does your leadership structure need to look like at twice your current revenue?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes a point that every scaling company needs to sit with: executives who do not deeply understand AI before deploying it across their organization are not managing a technology rollout. They are managing a risk they cannot see.

At Autobahn, we work with companies navigating the $50M to $500M journey, and the pattern is consistent. Leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who move fastest on new tools. They are the ones who know exactly what a tool demands of their organization before they commit to it.

AI is no different. It requires clear ownership, organizational readiness, and a leadership team willing to make hard calls about where it fits and where it does not.

post3.text:
When Strive Health announced it was expanding its executive team to scale its mission, the message underneath the press release was clear: growth at scale is a leadership challenge before it is anything else.

That is exactly what Katherine Slain addresses in Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It.

The chapter makes an uncomfortable argument that most leaders at growing companies are not leading at the level the business actually requires. Not because they lack capability, but because no one has shown them what leadership looks like when the stakes and the complexity both double.

Katherine draws on real experience with scaling companies to show what shifts when leaders stop managing their current reality and start building for the one coming next.

The insight that lands hardest is this: the people depending on you need a different version of your leadership than the one that got you here.

post1.text:
Most business owners think they'll maximize their exit value right before they sell. That is exactly backwards.

The multiple a buyer assigns your business has almost nothing to do with what you do in the final 12 months before a transaction. It reflects decisions you made three to five years earlier.

J.P. Morgan's Private Bank recently outlined how exit strategy shapes valuation long before a deal is on the table. The implication for $50M+ operators is significant.

Three things buyers actually pay a premium for:

1. Revenue that does not depend on the founder to exist. If you leave and the top line wobbles, your multiple shrinks.

2. Documented, repeatable processes. Buyers are acquiring a machine, not a collection of talented people.

3. Customer concentration below 20%. One client representing 30% of revenue is a liability priced into the offer.

Most owners wait too long to think about these levers. By then, the negotiating room has already closed.

If you sold your company today, which of these three would hurt you most?

post2.text:
A recent piece from BDC.ca made something very clear: the majority of entrepreneurs who say they are ready to exit their businesses are not actually prepared to do it.

That gap between readiness and preparation is where value gets destroyed.

At Autobahn Consultants, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and beyond. At that level, an unprepared exit does not just cost you a few percentage points. It can cost you tens of millions in final sale price.

Preparation means building transferable value now, not scrambling when a buyer appears. It means clean financials, leadership depth, and a growth story a buyer can verify.

If you are within five years of a potential exit, the time to start is today, not when the offer arrives.

Read the full BDC piece here and then ask yourself whether your business is actually exit-ready: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqAFBVV95cUxNS0lsdHVTMG5lenVwbDhBTXFBX2hUZnRhengxbWhrLU5LV210b2o3bFBvT3N5YllmMjVlYXJtcmxSS3ZZZFY5SlhibXVuZWxOMnRaUjVpbHhjUWhJc1V2TEljR05KdlZQaGY3elk0azk5OW9fY3RCQzBaaERqb2tEWFZPRUhYb1JuYkZqNjB2OW1Mb1NCbUNZQk85QmxjakhzRFhWR2huQ3A

post3.text:
Data keeps confirming what we see on the ground: business owners want to exit, but very few have built a company that earns the multiple they expect.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this directly. The chapter is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, and it was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two practitioners who have been inside these deals.

One thing they make clear early on: your valuation multiple is not a reward for longevity. It is a reflection of how transferable, predictable, and scalable your business actually is. Most owners conflate business success with exit readiness. Those are not the same thing.

If you are leading a company at $50M or beyond, this chapter will reframe how you think about every decision you make between now and your eventual exit.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ companies treat branding as decoration. It is not. It is infrastructure.

Ulta Beauty's CMO recently made clear that brand building and performance marketing are not competing priorities. They are the same investment, measured differently across different timelines. That distinction matters enormously for scaling companies that keep treating brand spend as something to cut when margins tighten.

Here is what leaders at your stage need to understand:

1. Your brand is already sending a signal. The question is whether you designed that signal or inherited it by accident.

2. Customers at $500M scale do not tolerate inconsistency. A brand that feels different across channels is a brand that feels untrustworthy.

3. Marketing strategy without brand strategy is just noise with a budget attached.

Campari has managed iconic brands across decades and multiple cultural shifts by treating brand identity as a living operating system, not a logo refresh. Companies scaling past $100M should think the same way.

What does your brand actually communicate to a customer who has never heard of you?

post2.text:
A recent piece in ADWEEK on how Campari manages heritage brands across cultural moments is worth a close read if you lead a company in growth mode.

The core tension Campari navigates is one every scaling business eventually faces: how do you preserve what made you credible while adapting to what your market actually looks like today? Get too rigid and you become a relic. Get too flexible and you lose the distinctiveness that earned trust in the first place.

For companies moving from $50M to $500M, this balance is not a brand question. It is a growth question. Your brand is either an asset that accelerates sales cycles or a liability that forces you to compete on price.

Read the full piece and ask yourself where your brand currently falls on that spectrum.

Authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West work with scaling companies every day, and their core argument is one that tends to surprise leaders: most companies at $50M already have a brand identity. post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

SHRM's recent research on hiring trends confirms what we see inside scaling companies every day: the firms winning on talent in 2026 are not the ones casting the widest net. They are the ones getting surgical about exactly who they need and why.

If you are running a $50M+ business, here is what that means in practice:

1. A hiring decision made without a clear performance profile is just an expensive guess. Define what great looks like before you post the role.

2. Speed-to-fill is a vanity metric. Time-to-productivity is the number that actually moves your business forward.

3. Your talent process should be as documented and repeatable as your sales process. If it lives in someone's head, you do not have a process.

Growth companies that scale well do not hire faster. They hire smarter, and they build the infrastructure to do it consistently.

What does your current hiring process actually optimize for?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business Wire announced that Ouster named a new Chief People Officer specifically to drive global growth and talent strategy.

This is worth paying attention to, and not because of the executive appointment itself.

It is because of the timing. Ouster is making a deliberate, public commitment to talent infrastructure as a growth lever, not as a back-office function.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this is the right instinct. The leaders who treat people strategy as a core business function, not an HR formality, are the ones who build organizations that can actually hold the weight of rapid growth.

If your people infrastructure is not keeping pace with your revenue ambitions, that gap will show up in execution before it shows up on your income statement.

Read the full announcement here: https://news.google.

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring and people infrastructure is not new to us. It is exactly what Chapter 6 of our upcoming book addresses head-on.

In "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," Chapter 6, called The Talent Engine, co-authored by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, goes deep on what it actually takes to build a talent function that scales with your business.

One thing Caleb, Darla, and Yasmin make clear: most companies at this stage have a talent process that works well enough until it suddenly does not. The insight is understanding when you are approaching that cliff, before your growth stalls and forces the lesson on you.

There is a framework inside this chapter that will change how you think about your next ten hires.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at $50M+ companies believe that tracking more metrics signals rigor. It actually signals a failure to prioritize. When everything is measured, nothing is acted on.

Business.com recently catalogued 14 different tools companies use to track KPIs. The tools are not the problem. The list is.

Here is what separates scaling companies from stalled ones on this topic:

1. The best leadership teams track 5 to 7 metrics maximum at the company level. Everything else lives downstream with the team responsible for it.

2. A KPI without an owner and a cadence is just a number on a dashboard nobody looks at.

3. Lagging indicators tell you what happened. If your weekly rhythm only reviews lagging indicators, you are running your business by looking in the rearview mirror.

The companies we see grow from $50M to $500M are ruthless about subtraction, not addition, when it comes to metrics.

How many KPIs does your leadership team actually review in a weekly meeting, and how many of those drive a real decision?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite breaks down 11 key KPIs hospitality companies should be tracking. It is a solid industry-specific resource, and the logic behind the selections is sound.

But here is what the article cannot tell you: knowing which KPIs to track and knowing which ones to act on are two completely different skills.

For companies scaling past $50M, the real danger is not a missing metric. It is a crowded scorecard where accountability gets diluted and leadership meetings turn into data reviews instead of decision sessions.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams to cut through the noise and build metric systems that create traction, not just reports.

Read the NetSuite piece and ask yourself which of your current KPIs would survive a ruthless cut.

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every leadership team running a $50M+ company needs to read before their next planning session.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled "Death by KPIs." It was written by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it tackles one of the most common traps growing companies fall into: measuring too much and managing too little.

One of the core ideas in the chapter is that KPI overload is not a data problem. It is a leadership clarity problem. The fix does not come from better software or bigger dashboards.

If your team spends more time building reports than making decisions, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong, and the productivity numbers prove it.

A recent Fortune survey found that 90% of executives say AI has not moved the needle on productivity. That is not an AI problem. That is a strategy problem.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. AI does not fix broken workflows. If your processes are inefficient at $50M, layering AI on top just automates the chaos faster.

2. The leaders actually seeing returns are not using AI company-wide. They are deploying it in targeted, high-leverage functions first, measuring the output, and then expanding.

3. Cutting headcount before proving AI-driven productivity gains is a bet, not a strategy. The companies that scale well treat AI as a growth lever, not a cost cutter.

Growth from $50M to $500M requires intentional decisions about where AI earns its place in your operation.

So here is the real question: Is your team using AI to accelerate a strong strategy, or to paper over a weak one?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bloomberg highlighted how 12 CEOs and senior executives are personally using AI to reclaim hours in their week. The tactics are practical, specific, and worth reading.

But here is what the article does not address: what works for an individual executive does not automatically translate into organizational productivity gains.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth range, the gap between a founder using AI effectively and a 200-person team doing the same is enormous. Closing that gap requires clear protocols, defined use cases, and leaders who model the behavior consistently.

AI fluency at the top is a starting point, not a finish line.

Read the Bloomberg piece and think about where your leadership team stands today: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxOc010ZUhURC0wVGNKMTdRUWVyTnZFVXRWODBxaVc3MWYyeU52bG1PdHVaTU45aS1mSG13Ulh2eUtmcU5qNXhma2VDLWo0UlpDLWMyU0lZc1ZkcHZzZXVrVXlpNGNObGVxRnVTMlVBc2RQLTk2bWtJaWFmeW1BMlBHNml5SktYdEdaLWJ3VmpYTU55bHB6cVpUVW5LWG1WR2lhRng0SXYwcHdFYXJTanJn?oc=5

post3.text:
Nine out of ten executives say AI has not improved productivity in their organizations. That number should stop every growth-stage leader in their tracks.

In Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, authors Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain dig into exactly why this disconnect happens and what to do about it.

The chapter introduces a framework for how scaling companies can move beyond AI experimentation and build it into the daily operating rhythm of their teams. One of the core ideas is that AI adoption is not a technology decision. It is a leadership decision, and it has to be treated that way from the top down.

If your company is growing fast and you are not sure whether your AI investments are actually working, this chapter was written for you.

The most capable leaders in the room are usually the ones most convinced they don't belong there.

That's not a flaw. It's a pattern.

Forbes Australia recently explored how impostor syndrome doesn't fade as leaders climb higher. If anything, it intensifies. More visibility, more stakes, more opportunities to feel exposed.

Here's what that means for leaders scaling companies past $50M:

1. The feeling of being 'found out' is not a signal to slow down. It's a signal that you're operating at the edge of your capability, which is exactly where growth lives.

2. Leaders who confuse self-doubt with incompetence make smaller bets, avoid key hires who outshine them, and stall the business. Leaders who normalize it make bolder moves.

3. At this revenue level, your psychology is a business variable. What you believe about yourself shapes your org chart, your pricing, your deals, and your ceiling.

The leaders who scale don't eliminate the doubt. They stop letting it make decisions.

So the real question is: how much is your inner critic actually running your company?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Seattle University outlines six practical ways leaders can push through impostor syndrome when stepping into new roles. The advice is solid and worth reading.

But here's the angle that matters most for companies scaling from $50M toward $500M: leadership transitions at this stage are constant. New divisions, new markets, new executive seats being filled. Every one of those moves puts someone in unfamiliar territory.

If your culture doesn't normalize the discomfort of not-yet-knowing, your best people will quietly shrink instead of grow into the roles you need them to fill.

Building psychological safety isn't a soft initiative. It's a scaling strategy.

There's a chapter in our upcoming book that asks a question most leaders won't ask out loud: how could you be successful and still feel like you don't deserve the seat?

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business, titled 'How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?', was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo. It goes somewhere most business books avoid entirely: the interior life of the leader driving the machine.

One insight the chapter surfaces is that impostor syndrome at scale isn't just personal. It leaks into decisions, team dynamics, and the pace of growth. The leader's unexamined self-doubt becomes an organizational constraint.

Knowing that changes how you lead. And how you scale.

post1.text:
Work-life balance is a trap. The leaders who scale companies past $100M don't balance their lives. They design them.

There is a difference. Balance implies equal weight on both sides of a scale. Design implies intention, trade-offs, and a plan you actually wrote down.

A recent TODAY.com feature on Latina entrepreneurs revealed something worth noting: the most resilient founders don't separate who they are from how they lead. Their personal values are the operating system, not a weekend hobby.

Here is what that looks like in practice for leaders at the $50M+ stage:

1. Your personal life plan should be reviewed on the same cadence as your business plan. Quarterly. Not annually.

2. Burnout at this level is rarely about hours. It is about misalignment between what you said matters and how you actually spend time.

3. The people around your executive team are part of your scaling strategy whether you acknowledge it or not.

The question is not how do you find more balance. The question is: have you ever actually designed your life, or have you just been reacting to it?

#LeadershipDevelopment #ScalingBusiness #ExecutiveLife

post2.text:
A recent piece in TODAY.com spotlighted five Latina entrepreneurs and the hard-won wisdom they carry into their businesses. One throughline stood out: sustainable success requires knowing who you are before the company tells you who to be.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth corridor, this is not a soft insight. It is a structural one.

Leaders who have never done the personal work tend to make decisions that serve their anxiety, not their strategy. They overhire, under-delegate, and conflate urgency with importance. The result is a company that scales their stress rather than their vision.

At Autobahn, we work with executives on exactly this. Growth requires the person at the top to be as intentional about their life as they are about their P&L.

A TODAY.com feature on entrepreneurial resilience got us thinking about a chapter we are particularly proud of in our upcoming book.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business is called Coming Up for Air. Co-authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, this chapter addresses something most business books skip entirely: what happens to the person leading the company while the company is growing.

One of the core ideas in this chapter is that scaling a business without a personal life plan is like building a highway with no exits. You will move fast, but you will not be able to stop when you need to.

Samantha brings a perspective in this chapter that reframes life planning not as a perk for when things slow down, but as a prerequisite for sustainable growth at the highest levels.
